alt: Dicey’s three ideas of the rule of law: no punishment without a breach proved in the ordinary courts, equality before the law, and rights secured by the ordinary law, illustrated by Entick v Carrington. The principle is applied to law making, the legal system and substantive law (A v Secretary of State for the Home Department).
caption: Three ideas from Dicey, tested in law making, the legal system and substantive law.

alt: A green paper consults and a white paper sets out proposals. The Bill passes First Reading, Second Reading, Committee Stage, Report Stage and Third Reading in each House, then receives Royal Assent. Below, the Parliament Acts let the Commons pass most Bills after about a year and money Bills after one month (War Crimes Act 1991, Hunting Act 2004, Jackson), and parliamentary supremacy means no court can invalidate an Act (Pickin).
caption: Five stages in each House, then Royal Assent; the Commons can override the Lords.

alt: An enabling Act gives power to make Orders in Council, statutory instruments and bylaws. Parliament controls them through consultation, affirmative and negative resolution and scrutiny committees; the courts by judicial review for procedural ultra vires (Aylesbury Mushrooms), substantive ultra vires (Public Law Project) and unreasonableness (Wednesbury; Strickland v Hayes). The Legislative and Regulatory Reform Act 2006 is noted.
caption: Delegated legislation exists only under an enabling Act, and both Parliament and the courts police it.

alt: Four approaches, each with its case: the literal rule (Whiteley v Chappell), the golden rule (Adler v George), the mischief rule (Smith v Hughes) and the purposive approach (Quintavalle). Purposive reading was encouraged by EU membership (Pickstone v Freemans) and by s3 Human Rights Act 1998 (Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza).
caption: From the plain words to the purpose: state the approach, cite the case, show the result.

alt: Three rules of language with their cases: ejusdem generis (Powell v Kempton Park), expressio unius (Tempest v Kilner) and noscitur a sociis (IRC v Frere). Intrinsic aids sit inside the Act; extrinsic aids, including Hansard, sit outside it. Pepper v Hart allows Hansard only where the words are ambiguous and a ministerial statement clearly resolves the point.
caption: Words take meaning from their neighbours; Hansard is a limited, conditional aid.

alt: The Supreme Court can depart from its own decisions under the Practice Statement 1966 (Herrington; Shivpuri). The Court of Appeal is bound by its own decisions except in the three Young v Bristol Aeroplane situations. Below: original precedent (Donoghue), persuasive precedent (James and Karimi following Holley), and avoidance by distinguishing (Balfour and Merritt), overruling and reversing.
caption: The Supreme Court uses the Practice Statement; the Court of Appeal has only the Young exceptions.
